newsitem.title: TANZANIA: IMF team applauds Tanzanian economic progress.
newsitem.headline: IMF team applauds Tanzanian economic progress.

text.p: Tanzanian success in cutting annualised inflation to 14 percent from 18 percent over a six-month period ranks among the best recent economic achievements in Africa, a senior IMF official said on Friday.
But IMF Deputy Director for Africa Goodall Gondwe and his visiting team from the Fund called for continuing fiscal discipline on the part of Tanzania's government.
Gondwe's team also expressed concern about the pace of Tanzania's privatisation programme and delays in implementing cuts to Tanzania's bloated civil service.

Latest figures from the central Bank of Tanzania showed a drop in annualised inflation to 14 percent in January from 15.4 percent in December and 18 percent in August, 1996. Annualised inflation in January, 1996 was running at 25.1 percent.
"This has been the best we've seen so far for Tanzania and compares favourably with the better performers in Africa," Gondwe told Reuters in an interview.
"It is hoped this performance is maintained as it could change very dramatically if discipline relaxes."

Gondwe heads a team of experts currently reviewing Tanzania's economic progress over a six month period following restoration of IMF credit in November. He said notable progress included cutting money supply and improved balance of payments.
Tanzania posted a trade deficit of $21.1 million in January, a fall of 77.8 percent versus $94.9 million the previous month.

"Balance of payments particularly, with reserves improving very substantially from 9.1 weeks of imports (August 1996) to close to 15.7 weeks in January (1997). That's a good six month result," Gondwe said.
Government revenue collection was also up and exceeded the benchmark target for Tanzania's Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) for six months ending December 31, 1996.
Actual revenue collected totalled 272 billion shillings compared to a target figure of 245 billion shillings.

Gondwe said the privatisation programme, part of the ESAF benchmark requirements, had been notable for its absence of large loss-making parastatals, listing Air Tanzania Corp, Tanzania Harbour Authority, and the state telecom monopoly, Tanzania Telecommunications Co Ltd.

"We (IMF) thought things could have gone better on the privatisation side. The sort of companies they are privatising were the smaller ones and one would like...a bigger impact on the economy by privatising the larger ones.

"Now, they're very much at the early stages of that and unfortunately when we came before (November 1996), they were still at the early stages. We don't think they've progressed much on that subject, even the president," Gondwe said.
Gondwe said despite these concerns, Tanzania was on target to receive its second ESAF tranche worth $35 million.
Last November, the IMF approved $240 million in credit after severing its support in 1992 over a tax scandal.

Tanzania is one of the world's poorest countries but in the 1980s emerged from two decades of disastrous socialist-inspired central planning and has gained a reputation as a state with a stable democracy and vast under-exploited potential.
